Some issues with editing, some issues with screenplay, loved mostly everything else. Tentatively a 7, will probably go up to an 8 on rewatch. Absolutely brilliant art direction, I loved the set design and the costume design, and I didn't even mind the CGI which even when obvious helped add to the visual surrealism of this movie. The cinematography is insane, every single frame of this movie makes it obvious that there is cinematography involved, and the film uses a very motivated wide selection of lenses to achieve this. I loved the really unconventional score as well. Emma Stone's performance is one of the best I've ever seen and she totally deserved the Oscar, Willem Dafoe is amazing as well (and the prosthetic make-up looks amazing), and I was shocked by how much I enjoyed Mark Ruffalo. Unfortunately I found this movie's commentary on womanhood and on wider society to be really shallow; far from offensive as others seem to find it, but not enough to drive the plot as long as it does. The movie is visually creative and entertaining enough to survive the long runtime anyway, but the screenplay struggles especially in the middle section. And while the editing mostly worked well on the small scale, it completely failed to communicate passage of time and left me very confused by the timeline of this film

Foi muito interessante acompanhar o amadurecimento de Bella ao longo da trama, principalmente no trecho do navio, em que ela se dá conta da existência da pobreza e de como a sociedade pode ser mesquinha e cruel com os mais pobres. Porém, a tentativa de tratar a sexualidade como a ferramenta central de libertação feminina acaba se perdendo ao longo da obra. Especialmente na fase em Paris, com a entrada na prostituição, o filme exagera na quantidade de cenas explícitas. O problema não é a presença do sexo na tela em si, mas sim a sua repetição exaustiva. Em vez de continuar desenvolvendo a mente e o intelecto em expansão de Bella, explorando sua forma única de descobrir o mundo, de construir afetos e de se relacionar com as pessoas, a direção prefere dar voltas no mesmo choque visual. Como dirigida por um homem, a experiência passa inevitavelmente pelo filtro do olhar masculino. Fica a nítida impressão de que a direção reduziu a "liberdade da mulher" a uma visão puramente corporal, esquecendo-se de que a descoberta de Bella já tinha ido muito além da sexualidade.

poor things was really good, don’t get me wrong, but i think my expectations were just WAY too high going into it. i’ve heard so much about this movie and expected to be completely blown away, so when i finished it i was more like “yeah… that was really good” instead of losing my mind over it. Emma Stone was incredible though. Bella is such a strange character, especially watching her go from basically having no understanding of the world to becoming more independent and forming her own ideas about everything. i loved how fearless and curious she was, and Emma fully committed to making her feel completely unlike a normal character. the visuals were also insane. the production design, costumes, sets, colours, the weird dreamlike look of everything… it genuinely feels like you’re watching a bizarre fairytale. Willem Dafoe and Mark Ruffalo were great too, and Ruffalo especially was so entertaining as Duncan. i think my biggest issue is just that i didn’t connect with it as much as i expected to. i could appreciate basically everything the movie was doing, but there were moments where i felt more impressed than emotionally invested. still, it’s creative, ambitious and definitely unlike most movies i’ve seen.

Une nouvelle interprétation du mythe de Prométhée mais autour d'un voyage initiatique. Bella Baxter apprend la vie, au sens où elle voit tous les vices de l'être humain mais aussi toutes ses qualités. Les personnages sont tous imparfaits mais cohérents, Max et Toinette semblant être les influences les plus positives sur Bella. Bella oscille donc entre modèles de vertu et modèles de perversité / corruption. Le tout dans une imagerie envoûtante et une réalisation rondement menée. Pas mon film favori mais un bon film qui peut parfois être un poil long sur certains actes.

In Yorgos Lanthimos’ Poor Things , Emma leaves ‘No Stone Unturned’. — Her pugnacious 👈🏻 (word of the day) Bella Baxter performance ‘kills two bird-dogs with one Stone’: 1. Fearless Physical Transformation: Emma Stone takes Bella Baxter from a reanimated child-like state to an articulate, autonomous woman with absolute physical precision. 2. Comedically Unpredictable Energy: Emma Stone handles Bella Baxter’s dark humour situations with an extremely funny attitude, but maintaining the importance of her character’s sympathetic circumstance. 👉🏻 Emma Stone in Yorgos Lanthimos films: 3 Oscar noms and 2 Oscar wins. 🏆 The Favourite (2018), Poor Things (2023), Bugonia (2025) My favourite scene: Duncan Wedderburn (Mark Ruffalo) and Bella are at a restaurant with a couple (Kitty and Gerald), eating oysters. Duncan asks Bella if she has had them before, and she replies she has not. After Bella tries an oyster, she immediately spits it out. Duncan Wedderburn: " Bella !" Bella Baxter: " Why keep it in my mouth if it is revolting? " Kitty: " I've said that before to Gerald. " For me, Emma Stone IS this movie . She brilliantly anchors a character defined by: 20% child-like discovery 60% sexual discovery 20% personal survival 🧠 🧠 🧠 🧠 out of 5 Mark Ruffalo — 🫵 👍🏻✌️ Cinematography is 🤪, 😵‍💫 and 😍

I need to offer something to the world and yet I have nothing. Comprendo la controversia con respecto a los temas que trata esta película. Es cierto que al menos al principio me chocó, pero creo que por describir ciertas situaciones no las está romantizando, justificando ni glorificando, sino incluso todo lo contrario. Durante toda la película Bella está en una constante guerra con lo que los hombres y la sociedad esperan de ella, intentando ser controlada de todas las formas posibles "recién nacida" en un mundo que no entiende. Que encontrase liberación personal de determinada manera no quita que esa vía que toma sea en sí misma un modo de explotación, y es más, hay un comentario que cuestiona esto en una escena. Sinceramente me la imaginaba mucho peor en este aspecto por lo que la gente comentaba, pero en mi opinión se tratan todos estos temas con precaución y astucia al mismo tiempo, sin que en ningún momento Bella pierda su autonomía ni su personalidad. A mí me ha flipado. Harry: Why do you stay with him? Bella: I always think it will be better. Brillante. Los juegos de cámara, las perspectivas, los escenarios y los vestuarios... Preciosos. Crea una atmósfera única. Trata muchísimas cuestiones muy diferentes (las injusticias, la naturaleza humana, las expectativas sociales, el matrimonio...) de manera interesante e ingeniosa. Papelón de Emma Stone. Aspiro a ser tan insoportable y despreocupada como Bella Baxter. I look at you and feel nothing but the lingering question: how did I ever want you?

Eu acho que não estava preparada para o quanto eu ia gostar de Pobres Criaturas. Comecei o filme sem saber direito o que esperar e terminei pensando em como uma história tão estranha conseguiu falar de coisas tão reais. Com certeza virou um dos meus filmes favoritos. A Bella é uma personagem muito diferente. No começo, ela está literalmente descobrindo o mundo, mas quanto mais ela conhece, mais começa a questionar tudo ao seu redor. E é justamente aí que o filme fica muito interessante: Bella não aceita que outras pessoas decidam o que ela pode ou não fazer. Pra mim, uma das maiores críticas do filme é justamente sobre a liberdade das mulheres. Durante toda a história, homens tentam controlar Bella, dizer o que ela deve fazer, como deve se comportar e até o que ela deve sentir. Só que, conforme ela conhece o mundo, ela percebe que não precisa viver dentro dessas regras. Ela quer conhecer, experimentar, errar e escolher por si mesma. E gosto muito que o filme não transforme essa liberdade em algo perfeito ou bonito o tempo inteiro. Bella toma decisões que podem ser consideradas erradas, passa por situações desconfortáveis e descobre coisas difíceis, mas ainda assim são experiências que pertencem a ela. Pela primeira vez, ela está vivendo a própria vida, e não a vida que alguém escolheu por ela. A estética também é uma das coisas que mais me conquistaram. Tudo parece um sonho meio estranho: os cenários, as cores, as roupas e até os movimentos da câmera. É exagerado e bizarro, mas combina perfeitamente com a forma como Bella enxerga o mundo. E a Emma Stone está simplesmente perfeita. A atuação dela faz a evolução da Bella parecer muito natural, principalmente porque conseguimos perceber a personagem mudando aos poucos, sem ela perder aquela personalidade curiosa e completamente fora do padrão. No final, Pobres Criaturas acabou sendo um filme que eu não esperava amar tanto. É estranho, engraçado, desconfortável e bonito ao mesmo tempo, mas principalmente é uma história sobre uma mulher descobrindo que ela tem o direito de escolher o próprio caminho. Virou facilmente um dos meus filmes favoritos, e acho que é daqueles que ficam na cabeça muito depois dos créditos.

Poor Things: Slut-Shaming Happening Both Onscreen and Off When a film receives such high praise while simultaneously stirring up so much controversy, where exactly does the problem lie? Is it the film itself, the audience, or even society at large? The movie is saturated with explicit sex scenes—some have gone so far as to call it pornography, saying "male audiences are having the best time." Others have gone further, questioning whether the film is a faux-feminist work riddled with the male gaze (their reasoning being that both the screenwriter and director are men). Yes, the male gaze is indeed pervasive—but it comes from a portion of the audience's own male gaze, as well as from a strain of feminism so pedantic it engages in self-imposed moral policing. A feminism that stigmatizes sex and refuses to engage with it is, in truth, still thinking through a patriarchal lens. (1) Only "Sluts" Exist, Never "Man-Whores"? "The sexuality of a woman as private property is moral; the sexuality of a woman as a subject is immoral." This notion almost fundamentally encapsulates the logic behind most of the moral criticism surrounding this film. From a modern societal perspective, attaching moral constraints to sex is perfectly reasonable—the problem is that rather than applying such standards equally to everyone, patriarchy's stigmatization of sex is aimed specifically at women. So when audiences watch Bella on the big screen masturbating without an ounce of shame, having sex with various men, and actively choosing to become a prostitute, plenty of viewers conclude that Bella is a "slut." They see her becoming a sex worker as a form of self-objectification—even though Bella is far from ordinary, possessing none of society's ingrained moral constructs. She masturbates simply for pleasure; her sexual encounters with various men are entirely consensual—she is, as a subject, freely unleashing her desires. (Setting aside the question of whether unrestrained indulgence is justifiable, the key point here is subject versus object.) Yet audiences still insist on seeing her as an object, convinced that she has been reduced to a product whose purpose is to please men with sex. They believe that female sexual liberation is a form of self-deception, that in the end women are still being "taken advantage of" by men. So the film's abundant display of the female lead's sexual scenes actually carries no inherent sense of the gaze—it is simply presentation. Yet many female viewers feel uncomfortable with the sex scenes in the film, developing a sense that these scenes come from a male-gaze perspective. In reality, it's because they have preemptively placed themselves in the position of the object, the passive party—a mindset that presupposes oneself as the victim. So when they see the female lead's sex scenes, and it happens that the director is male, they begin to conspiracy-theorize that patriarchal forces are trying to reap benefits by encouraging female sexual liberation. They think the film is patriarchy's sugar-coated trap—but in truth, patriarchy's trap was already planted in their own minds long ago. It's worth noting that the rakish lawyer Duncan in the film proudly boasts about having slept with many women. No one morally condemns him for it. Offscreen, men are likewise never shamed for having extensive sexual experience—on the contrary, they're seen as "impressive." And yet this same Duncan still believes he has the right to criticize Bella as a slut. So it turns out only "sluts" exist—never "man-whores." (2) Enlightenment Through Prostitution? One of the film's most controversial plot points is Bella actively choosing to become a prostitute—and clearly maturing and growing through that experience. This has led many to crudely interpret it as the director suggesting that prostitution can foster a woman's intellectual growth. Admittedly, the film's chosen mode of expression is provocative, but this prostitution episode is more symbolic of what the world perceives as "depravity." "We must experience everything—not just the good, but depravity, fear, and sorrow too." This doesn't mean we all need to become sex workers; rather, it means that experiencing hardship does indeed open the door to a person's inner world of thought and spirit. Someone who has only ever experienced pleasant things is destined never to become a mature person capable of deep reflection. (3) Is the Film Advocating Sexual Liberation? What About Social Systems? So the film does explore desire, but its purpose is not to advocate unbridled indulgence. And desire comes in many forms—sex is merely one dimension of it. But undeniably, sex delivers the greatest visual impact, and shattering ingrained perceptions requires a certain degree of shock. Therefore, the film's abundance of sexual imagery is not trying to say that sexual liberation is the most important pillar of feminism, nor is it attempting to obscure other issues. It isn't even really a feminist film—one might sooner call it a libertarian film that takes a passing jab at patriarchy. Don't forget that Bella is an infant in a fully grown body, devoid of society's ingrained moral constructs, utterly loyal to her own instincts and desires. We can never become Bella. Rather, through the shock that Bella's behavior delivers to us, we become aware of how much society's concepts restrict our thinking—how they keep us trapped in perpetual cycles of self-moralizing and judging others. As a surreal film with absurdist themes, it is destined to be considered immoral by society's moral standards. Fixating on that point yields little of value. We don't need to—and cannot—become Bella, nor do we need to impose moral constraints on Bella or the film. But that doesn't stop me from intuitively finding something beautiful in Bella's purity. Ultimately, a film can never change society. When it tries to point out the absurdity of certain social rules, the public turns around and accuses it of being heretical. Perhaps it is destined to be something the masses cannot understand—poor things, pointing straight at you and me.
